> **DannyBruza:** tommy sorry that you could not see the site...my i ask why type system and brouser..... we do intend to make a just text and photos site.. that one's who cant see the site can go to.....we were trying to make the site very cutting edge....and most of systems can see flash....mabe it would be good to put link to flashplugin too....... Ive tried the site on Netscape and microsoft......and had no problems.....i wish everyone used the same standards....but sense that won't happen i try my best to keep it cutting edge and yet versatile to most platform's

As far as standards, that is W3C's and the IETF's call. And flash is no standard.

I use a browser named konqueror, its part of KDE, and it meets all the appropriate W3C and IETF standards. If it was failing to render an HTML file (IE: a file that can be generated by the HTML grammar which W3C has distributed (just because it "works" dosn't mean its correct)) or something like a jpeg (an ISO standard) then its my bad. The problem is the files you created don't use real anchor tags. They aren't HTML.

The holography forum has a flash animation at the top. I've never actualy seen it. However it doesn't impede the usefulness of the site. The eye candy dosn't have to break things.

The entire point of the web was to get rid of needing specific software to look at content beyond flat text. All this "cutting edge" stuff does is bring back the bad old days of no one being able to share anything, except to others with exactly the same computer, applications, and matching versions.

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md: > boy you guys are pickey HAHAHAHA! Danny, you ain't seen "picky" just yet... Tommy, thank you for pointing out the cross-platform/browser/system/etc incompatibilities. I can't see any fireworks either, in fact, when I load the site in my preferred browser here's what I see: [http://www.9000shops.com/tripletake.jpg](http://www.9000shops.com/tripletake.jpg) Yeah, I'm going to buy a lot of stuff from that site. So will lots of others. See any problem there? I've pointed out the reason for that, but I guess I'm the only one that's seeing it(?) I don't claim to be an expert in the use of the web, but does anyone else here make their living on internet sales? I do. While my knowledge of the latest code has fallen years behind, I try to write code that can be viewed on any computer that can surf the web (webtv is another matter, but I get orders from those users too), even if it's running windows 3.11. That's become more difficult as the standards change, but all our code is done by hand, clean and short as possible. Where'd all the bandwidth go? Things like big fat css references that could have been handled with under 100 characters, pointless java, etc. It shouldn't take a 50k file to load a page that says "click here". It seems to me that the site, while cool-looking in a browser that can see it (I can see it in my non-preferred browser, Netscape 7 [aka: "monkeydung"], yes, it's been cool looking all along), violates one of the basic tenets of sales: Don't do anything that prevents customers from buying. If you want to sell stuff to fat people, you don't make them climb a 12 foot rock wall to get to it. So I need to install the latest Flash plugin? Why? YOU want to SELL to ME (or anybody, anywhere). I shouldn't have to do anything but give you money, it's your job to figure out how to get it, not how to NOT get it. If the flying clowns stop people from getting to the merchandise, it's time to fire them. I can understand wanting the site to be "cutting-edge", but the only time that it's logical for a site to be cutting edge is when that's what you're selling ("cutting-edge"). If you want my sister, who's got a little money but the brains of a can of Alpo, to buy anything, you'll be out of luck. Remember, not everyone is a techie, and plenty of Windows users are afraid to install *anything* new that isn't absolutely essential. Ok, so it works on your machine, and I can get it to work on my machine. What about the rest? I sell to a broad cross section of society, ages from pre-teen to 70+, poor folks to district court judges and actual scientists, and looking at my site platform report, all manner of computer users. Platforms recorded in our recent stats include: Win XP, Win 98, Win 2000, Win ME, Mac PPC, Mac 68k, Win 95, Win NT, Linux x86, WebTV, Win Server 2003, Linux, Win 3.1, Sun OS, Amiga, Unix, BeOS, CP/M-80, FreeBSD, FreeBSD x86, NetPliance, OS/2, Open BSD, QNX, RISC OS, and Nokia Web Telephone. Browsers from the same stats include 26 pages of listings, I assume mostly robots but it includes a substantial component of older browsers (and, incidentally, 599 hits through "Konqueror 3.x") The foregoing data is based on 224,213 site visits, 4,225,096 total actual hits, and 33.8 gigabytes transferred, to users in 102 countries. Oh, and what do I sell? If you haven't seen it, hold on to your chair: [http://www.riorondo.com](http://www.riorondo.com) So, why do you need to watch out for too much Flash? Because if it stops people from buying from a sales oriented site, it's a bad thing, no matter how cool it looks. Ok, so enough of my stupid opinion, I've only spent about fifteen years selling various crap, and the rest making it. On to bitching about the site itself, more of a bug report: Everything really needs to be spelled correctly. What are "holograpms"? Check that first button on the left. Or is it my browser? When I click on the "classes" button on the left side, the page that comes up is missing the block of four buttons above it. When I click the "ask-dinesh" button, the page comes up with the button block centered in the middle of the page instead of being on the left where it belongs. Please capitalize "Dinesh". Let's hope the questions that come in from that link don't drive him completely insane ("will you market my 'photon-paddleball' set?", "What do photons taste like?") The "photos" section is a little clunky. Needs to have the photos link bar on all the photo pages so you don't have to hit the "back" button to look at another set. Same thing with products, should be able to jump across the bottom levels. (buy-buy-buy!) Now, if anyone's read this far, let me stress that the artwork is great (where'd those wavy buttons go?) and that I think Danny's done a wonderful job on producing the site (better looking than I'd be able to make it). My primary objection is that there's all this fluff, but almost no content. I'm from southern California, I used to know a lot of people that were like that - looked great but had all the underlying substance of styrofoam packing material. My other objection is that it seems that anyone who actually wanted to BUY anything would have to hunt around to figure out how to do that. Since I'd like to see the business succeed, I'd think that sales should be the number one priority. Anyplace I've sold stuff, that's been our reason to exist. Keep it simple, go there-pay money-get stuff-done. The product section does look pretty good, get that "buying stuff" part up there! If I've offended anyone I apologize, but consider the content. Oh, and I heard a new (to me) term: Heisenbugs - the source of problems that only disappear when you search for them specifically. -Gary

I have been quiet on this matter but thought I should chime in. I too fully agree that a site or at least the first page should have a branch in it (two links) only. Check out this high tech company and how simple but elegant their site is. I used to work for them and their philosophy was keep is simple and let the simplicity pay for the fluff and research. BTW, they sell pinholes and I can tell you from experience these are pinholes are of superior quality. 

[http://www.lenoxlaser.com/](http://www.lenoxlaser.com/)

Also another idea may be to have the products page come up first with simple images of all the products with three options under each, one fora link to an enlarged view, another for a link to an animated movie file of the hologram viewed from different angles and a third with price. Also the price should be directly under these small images and how to order should be on that page also, clearly and easily found.

Don't get me wrong, the site is looking really great and I see all the bells and whistles but if I wanted to buy a hologram off that site, I surely would not want a low bandwidth connection as it takes time to navigate and find my way around.

Peace, and don't be discouraged, you are doing great work and hopefully the feedback you are getting helps broaden your perspective on what people want/need and will fertilize your work into growing into something fruitful.

PS: Before you publish a page, can you get someone to check your spelling, grammar and punctuation?

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
Nice work Danny, sorry about the rant. It seems like you made a site for holographers, while the real object is to sell to the masses (more or less). Make it easy for them.

I have a couple of other suggestions:

That "grey screen" thing remains a problem, but will only be solved by:

A. Getting that referring host to slightly alter the frames code they use - my preferred browser isn't *that* old.

B. Getting an actual hosted domain, as I've noted before. Should be doable for under $20/month, I think ours is about $26/mo and we've got secure forms processing, SSL, and other stuff. See comment below. Paying for domain hosting is like paying for shoes - it's worth it.

Build a FAQ. If I send model horse folk, they're going to ask questions that shouldn't need to be answered more than once or twice, like "How much to make a hologram of my model horse", "How much to make a hologram of my real live horse", and "Can you put a hologram ON my model horse". Building a FAQ will help keep Dinesh from going insane when the "elves" ask the same asinine questions over and over.

Build a "suggestion box". This to shunt the "You should do X" comments off to a list that's easy to read, manage, and ignore if need be, and helps keep the number of site related emails down. It looks like ipowerweb.net, who appears to be hosting 4s-c.org, could handle the domain and provide the server side processing to cover all that, and apparently for cheap. I only write server-side code for NetCloak, but I imagine they've got some samples that could be adjusted.

 Oh, and bury any email addresses in code, preferably using a form that sends to the server which THEN sends the email. Email addresses are gleaned by robots and can result in upwards of 300 spam emails per day (like I get!).

 That's all I can remember right this second. What's that "store" part going to be? Shopping cart? Paypal related? Host based? Paying for an external card processor? (hope not)

Some of this might seem like it should be sent through private emails, but I'm doing it here because there's bound to be people more expert than I who might chime in where it would be valuable.

 -Gary
